comment.narrative: The baseline quantitative values are zero at this point as this indicator defines an increase. 8/40 reported to have ever participated in political campaigns; 6/40 reported to to have run for political office; 14/40 women interviewed at baseline reported they are interested in political affairs, 19/40 reported having knowledge on both electoral and governance process and only 1/40 perceive that the political process is fair for women aspirants because of high levels of illiteracy; low levels of education, awareness of women’s rights, and self-esteem; lack of energy/time outside of economic activities; and high rates of VAW/G.Sudan’s female population is culturally diverse and subject to different religious beliefs, social andeconomic positions and ethnicities. However, women are bound by common unequal access toeducation, health care and political representation, and gendered roles which are reinforced bycultural norms, religion, societal perceptions, socialization processes, and patriarchal practices25The socio-economic context continues to be plagued by increasing poverty compounded bywidespread gendered unemployment. Women are generally highly marginalized from the labormarket and are comparatively more likely to be unemployed. In 2014 for instance, womenparticipation in the labor force was 33% compared to 76% of men, and women were more thantwice as likely to be unemployed as compared to men.26 Sudan population is very young with 60%of the population below the age of 25. Nearly half of unemployed Sudanese are under 25, and disproportionately women, with female youth 55% less likely to be employed compared to femaleadults. Women have less than a third of the legal rights men have vis a viz access to economicopportunities, which ranks Sudan near the bottom of the Global Women, Business, and the Law2021 index.

We are targeting 90 women from 3 regions who are part of the already established GENs (Gender Equality Networks). We will work towards reducing the barriers to women's participation in decision making processes including illiteracy; low levels of education, awareness of women’s rights, and self-esteem; lack of energy/time outside of economic activities; and high rates of VAW/G.
